newsitem.title: GERMANY: Military planners seek to build consensus on Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Military planners seek to build consensus on Zaire.

text.p: Western and African military leaders sought on Saturday to establish how many refugees needed help in Zaire in order to develop military options.

Talks between nations interested in contributing to an anticipated military mission resumed on Saturday after an initial meeting on Friday when aid groups failed to agree on the number of refugees at risk in the region.

"No decision has yet been taken on the number of refugees," said Lieutenant Commander Louis Garneau, a spokesman for the Canadian military delegation at the meeting at the U.S. European Command in Stuttgart.

Lieutenant-General Maurice Baril of Canada, coordinating the U.N.-authorised mission, told a news conference on Friday that estimates presented at the meeting of the number of refugees in need of help varied from 100,000 to 500,000.
"We're going to find out (how many there are) before we commit any troops," he said. "By the end of the weekend I would hope we will have developed a full slate of options."

After the talks ended on Friday night, Baril denied there was friction between commanders and the aid group representatives, who have provided higher estimates of the refugee population than those from the military.
"It is not because we have different opinions but that we have different sources of information. They (the aid group representatives) have been away from the refugees for many days," Baril said.
The Stuttgart meeting is expected to consider various military options but leave the final decision to individual governments.

Three scenarios in a preliminary discussion document seen by Reuters set out the pros and cons of basing a military relief operation in Rwanda or in Zaire and included a third option of not sending any extra troops at all.
A military official at the talks confirmed the paper was the basis for early discussions by the planners.

It noted many nations were ready to provide relief from a base in Rwanda, and the option would probably only need light security. But it would require approval from Rwanda, which has so far been reluctant to see an operation on its soil.
Providing relief from a base in Zaire would mean establishing a secure headquarters, probably with heavy forces.
The paper said the idea had support from the Zairean government, but carried a bigger risk of becoming embroiled in regional conflict.
The option would limit efforts to repatriate Hutu refugees who fled from Rwanda in 1994, according to the papers.
It would also need more complex logistical suppport than a Rwanda-based operation, and take more time.
In a third option, external forces would maintain low-level operational help they now give to Rwanda and relief agencies.

The official, who asked not to be named, said it was likely att the options would undergo extensive revision during the course of the meeting but only after a consensus had been built on the number of refugees at risk.
Baril refused to be drawn on how many troops, if any, a mission might require, but said there appeared to be between 100,000 and 250,000 refugees requiring help.

A major problem for nations wanting to help has been the fluidity of the situation in eastern Zaire, where hundreds of thousands of Rwandan Hutu refugees have been displaced by a conflict pitting Rwandan-backed Zairean Tutsi rebels against Zairean government forces and Rwandan Hutu militias.
U.S. Brigadier General John Casey said on Friday that one problem was finding out how many displaced people were Rwandan refugees and not Zaireans displaced within their own country.

But Baril played down the distinction between the people, saying: "If we have people starving within our region of operation, we don't care if they are refugees or displaced. We are going to feed them."
